sentences: In an island beach town, a young woman goes for a late-night ocean swim.
An unseen force attacks and pulls her underwater.
Her partial remains are found washed up on the beach the next morning.
After the coroner concludes it was a shark attack, the town's police chief plans to close the beaches.
The mayor persuades him to reconsider, fearing the town's summer economy will suffer.
The coroner, apparently under pressure, now concurs with the mayor's theory that it was a boating accident.
The police chief reluctantly accepts their conclusion until a young boy is killed at a crowded beach.
A $3,000 bounty is placed on the shark, causing an amateur shark-hunting frenzy.
An eccentric local shark hunter offers his services for $10,000.
A consulting oceanographer examines the woman's remains, confirming she was killed by an unusually large shark.
When local fishermen catch a tiger shark, the mayor declares the beaches safe.
The skeptical oceanographer dissects the shark and, finding no human remains inside its stomach, concludes the killer shark is still active.
While searching the night waters in the oceanographer's boat, the oceanographer and the police chief find the half-sunken boat of a local fisherman.
The oceanographer dons a scuba suit and goes underwater to check the boat's hull and finds a large shark tooth embedded into it.
He drops the tooth after encountering the fisherman's severed head.
The mayor dismisses the police chief and the oceanographer's assertions that a great white shark caused the deaths and refuses to close the beaches, allowing only increased safety precautions.
On the Fourth of July weekend, tourists pack the beaches.
The shark enters a nearby lagoon, killing a boater and nearly killing the police chief's son, who is hospitalized with shock.
The police chief then convinces a guilt-ridden mayor to hire the shark hunter.
Despite initial tension between the shark hunter and the oceanographer, and the police chief's fear of the ocean, the three head out to sea on the shark hunter's boat to hunt for the shark.
As the police chief lays down a chum line, the shark suddenly appears behind the boat.

The shark hunter, estimating it is 25 feet (7.6 m) long and weighs 3 tonnes (3.0 long tons; 3.3 short tons), harpoons it with a line attached to a flotation barrel, but the shark pulls it underwater and disappears.
At nightfall, the shark hunter and the oceanographer drunkenly exchange stories about their assorted body scars.
One of the shark hunter's is a removed tattoo; he reveals that during World War II, he survived the sinking of a navy ship, during which sharks killed many sailors.
The shark returns, ramming the boat's hull and disabling the power.
The men work through the night, repairing the engine.
In the morning, the police chief attempts to call the coast guard, but the shark hunter, obsessed with killing the shark without outside assistance, smashes the radio.
After a long chase, the shark hunter harpoons the shark with another barrel.
The line is tied to the stern cleats, but the shark drags the boat backward, swamping the deck and flooding the engine compartment.
As the shark hunter is about to sever the line to save the boat's transom, the cleats break off; the barrels stay attached to the shark.
To the police chief's relief, the shark hunter speeds the boat toward shore to draw the shark into shallower waters, but the damaged engine fails.
As the boat takes on water, the trio attempt a riskier approach.
The oceanographer suits up and enters a shark-proof cage, intending to lethally inject the shark with strychnine via a hypodermic spear.
The shark attacks the cage, causing the oceanographer to drop the spear.
While the shark destroys the cage, the oceanographer escapes to the ocean bottom.
The shark leaps onto the boat's stern, subsequently devouring the shark hunter.
Trapped on the sinking vessel, the police chief thrusts a scuba tank into the shark's mouth and climbing onto the crow's nest shoots the tank with a rifle.
The resulting explosion kills the shark.
The oceanographer resurfaces, and he and the police chief paddle back to shore, clinging to the remaining barrels.
In December 1941, an American expatriate owns a nightclub and gambling den in a city, then in French territory.
The club owner's café attracts a varied clientele, including French and German officials, refugees desperate to reach a still-neutral country, and those who prey on them.
Although the club owner professes to be neutral in all matters, he ran guns abroad in 1935 and fought on the republican side in the Spanish civil war.
A petty crook boasts to the club owner of letters of transit obtained by murdering two German couriers.
The papers allow the bearers to travel freely around German-occupied territory and to a neutral country.

The crook plans to sell them at the club and persuades the club owner to hold them for him; however, the crook is arrested by the local police under their captain, the unabashedly corrupt prefect of police.
The crook is killed while in custody without revealing that the club owner has the letters.
Then, the reason for the club owner's cynical nature—his former lover—enters his establishment.
Spotting the club owner's friend and house pianist, the woman asks him to play a song.
The club owner storms over, furious that the pianist disobeyed his order to never perform that song again, and is stunned to see the woman.
She is accompanied by her husband, a renowned fugitive Czechoslovak resistance leader.
A flashback reveals the woman left the club owner without explanation when the couple were planning to flee as the German army neared another city in 1940, embittering the club owner.
The resistance leader and the woman need the letters to escape, while a German major arrives in the city to prevent that.
When the resistance leader makes inquiries, an underworld figure and the club owner's friendly business rival divulges his suspicion that the club owner has the letters.
The resistance leader returns to the club owner's café that night and tries to buy them.
The club owner refuses to sell, telling the resistance leader to ask his wife why.
They are interrupted when the major leads a group of German officers in singing a song.
The resistance leader orders the house band to play another song, and the club owner allows it.
Patriotism grips the crowd and everyone joins in, drowning out the Germans.
Afterwards, the major has the captain close the club on a flimsy pretext.
Later, the woman confronts the club owner in the deserted café; when he refuses to give her the letters, she threatens him with a gun but then confesses she still loves him.
She explains that when they met and fell in love in the other city, she believed her husband had been killed while attempting to escape from a concentration camp.
When she learned that the resistance leader was alive and in hiding, she left the club owner without explanation to nurse her sick husband.
The club owner's bitterness dissolves.
He agrees to help, letting the woman believe she will stay with him, while the resistance leader leaves the city.
When the resistance leader unexpectedly shows up, having narrowly escaped a police raid on a resistance meeting, the club owner has a waiter spirit the woman away.
The resistance leader, aware of the club owner's love for the woman, tries to persuade him to use the letters to take her to safety.

When the police arrest the resistance leader on a trumped-up charge, the club owner persuades the captain to release him by promising to set the resistance leader up for a much more serious crime: possession of the letters.
To allay the captain's suspicions, the club owner explains that he and the woman will use the letters to leave for another country.
When the captain tries to arrest the resistance leader as arranged, however, the club owner forces him at gunpoint to assist in their escape.

At the last moment, the club owner makes the woman board the plane to another city with the resistance leader, telling her that she would regret it if she stayed, "Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, but soon and for the rest of your life."
The major, tipped off by the captain, drives up alone.
The major attempts to stop the plane and then draws a gun on the club owner; the latter shoots him dead.
When policemen arrive, the captain pauses, then orders them to "round up the usual suspects."
He suggests to the club owner that they join the French forces in another city.
As they walk away into the fog, the club owner says, "Captain, I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship."
During the late 18th century in the country, a couple and their five daughters live at their rural estate in the county.
The mother, eager to secure suitable marriages for her daughters, is delighted when a wealthy bachelor moves into a nearby hall.
At an assembly ball, the bachelor, his sister, and his gentleman friend meet the local society.
The bachelor and the eldest daughter are immediately taken with each other, while the heroine instantly dislikes the snobbish gentleman and overhears his dismissive remarks about her.
Later, visiting the bachelor and his sister, the eldest daughter falls ill and must stay to recuperate.
While the heroine is visiting the eldest daughter at the hall, she verbally spars with the bachelor's haughty sister and the aloof gentleman.

The eldest daughter recovers and, soon after, the father's cousin, a pompous clergyman, visits the family; as the closest male relative, the clergyman will inherit the estate as it is entailed on the male line.

The clergyman tells the mother he intends to propose to the eldest daughter, but she says the eldest daughter will soon be engaged and suggests the heroine, whom the clergyman considers an agreeable alternative.
The sisters also meet a handsome and charming soldier, whose father worked for the gentleman's family.
He wins the heroine's sympathy by telling her that the gentleman denied him his rightful inheritance.
At the ball at the hall, the heroine dances with the gentleman, though the encounter is strained.
The next day, the clergyman proposes to the heroine, who roundly rejects him; despite her mother's anger, her father supports her decision.
The heroine is astonished when her close friend, fearing spinsterhood, announces her engagement to the clergyman.
The bachelor's party unexpectedly returns to the city.
The heroine urges the eldest daughter to visit their aunt and uncle, who live in the city, hoping she reconnects with the bachelor.
Months later, the heroine visits her friend and the clergyman, who reside next to a noblewoman's estate in another county.
The heroine unexpectedly meets the gentleman, who is the noblewoman's nephew and visiting with his cousin, a colonel.
Unaware that the eldest daughter is the heroine's sister, the colonel mentions that the gentleman recently untangled the bachelor from an imprudent match with an "unsuitable" family.
Distraught, the heroine is then met by the gentleman, who to her amazement proposes marriage, declaring his ardent love despite her inferior rank and family.
Offended and angry, she refuses him.
He defends separating the eldest daughter and the bachelor, believing the eldest daughter indifferent to his friend, and criticises the rest of her family's occasional social impropriety.
The heroine also cites his mistreating the soldier.

Angry and heartbroken, the gentleman delivers the heroine a letter describing the soldier's true character: the soldier squandered the bequest the gentleman's father left him, then attempted to seduce the gentleman's 15-year-old sister into eloping to gain her fortune.
The heroine returns home, as does the eldest daughter.
Accompanying her aunt and uncle on a trip to another region, the heroine reluctantly tours the grand estate of the gentleman's family in another county.
She unexpectedly runs into the gentleman, who invites her and her aunt and uncle to dine there.
The gentleman's manner has softened considerably, impressing her aunt and uncle, and his sister shares her brother's flattering reports about the heroine.
An urgent letter from the eldest daughter reveals that the youngest daughter has run off with the soldier.
The gentleman leaves abruptly, and the heroine returns home, certain she will never see the gentleman again.
Her mother fears the youngest daughter's disgrace will ruin her other daughters' chances of good marriages.
After a tense waiting period, her uncle sends news that the youngest daughter and the soldier are now married, and the newlyweds return to the family estate.
The youngest daughter lets slip to the heroine that it was the gentleman who found them and paid for their wedding; he also purchased the soldier's military commission.
The bachelor and the gentleman return to the hall and visit the family estate.
The bachelor proposes to the eldest daughter, who accepts.

Late that night, the noblewoman arrives to see the heroine and demands she never become engaged to the gentleman because, she claims, the gentleman has been engaged to marry the noblewoman's daughter, who has suffered poor health since infancy.
Deeply insulted, the heroine orders her to leave.
Walking early the next morning, the heroine encounters the gentleman, who apologises for his aunt's intrusion.
He professes his continued love and the heroine, her feelings radically altered, accepts his proposal.
She tells her father the truth of the gentleman's actions, and her father gives the heroine his consent to marry, overjoyed she has found love.
An industrialist has created an animal theme park featuring de-extinct dinosaurs, on a tropical island off the coast of a country.
After a Velociraptor kills a dinosaur handler, the park's investors, represented by a lawyer, threaten to pull funding unless experts certify the island's safety.
The lawyer invites a chaotician, while the industrialist invites a paleontologist and a paleobotanist.
Upon arrival, the group is shocked to see living Brachiosaurus and Parasaurolophus.
At the park's visitor center, the group learns that the cloning was accomplished by extracting dinosaur DNA from prehistoric mosquitoes preserved in amber.
DNA from frogs and other animals was used to fill in gaps in the dinosaurs' genome.
To prevent the dinosaurs from breeding, they are all made female by chromosome manipulation.
The group witnesses the hatching of a baby Velociraptor and visits the raptor enclosure.
During lunch, they debate the ethics of cloning and of the park in general.
The chaotician warns of the implications of genetic engineering while the paleontologist and the paleobotanist express uncertainty over the ability of humans and dinosaurs to coexist.
The industrialist's grandchildren join the others for a park tour in two self-driving electric vehicles, while the industrialist observes them from the control room.
Most of the dinosaurs fail to appear, and the paleobotanist stays behind to study a sick Triceratops.
The tour is cut short as a tropical storm approaches.
The park employees leave for the mainland on a boat while the visitors return to their vehicles.
The park's disgruntled computer programmer was previously bribed to steal frozen dinosaur embryos by a man working for the industrialist's corporate rival.
To access the embryo storage room, the programmer deactivates the park's security system, cutting power to the tour vehicles.
Most of the park's electric fences have been deactivated, which allows a Tyrannosaurus rex to escape and attack the touring group.
The Tyrannosaurus devours the lawyer and injures the chaotician while the paleontologist and the grandchildren escape.
On his way to deliver the embryos to the island's docks, the programmer gets lost in the rain, crashes his jeep, and is killed by a venom-spitting Dilophosaurus.
The paleobotanist helps the game warden search for survivors; they find the chaotician just before the Tyrannosaurus returns and chases them away.
The paleontologist and the grandchildren take shelter in a tree and encounter a Brachiosaurus herd, discovering the broken shells of dinosaur eggs the following morning.
The paleontologist concludes that the dinosaurs are breeding, which is possible because of their amphibian DNA—amphibians like West African frogs can change their sex in a single-sex environment.
Unable to decipher the programmer's code to reactivate the security system, the industrialist and the chief engineer decide to reboot the park's systems.
They shut down the power grid and retreat to an emergency bunker while the chief engineer heads to a maintenance shed to complete the rebooting process.
When the chief engineer fails to return, the paleobotanist and the game warden go to the shed, and discover that the shutdown has released the Velociraptors.
The paleobotanist turns the power back on before being attacked by a raptor and discovering the chief engineer's severed arm.
While she escapes, the game warden is killed by another Velociraptor.
The paleontologist and the grandchildren reach the visitor center.
The paleontologist leaves to look for the paleobotanist, leaving the grandchildren inside.
The raptors appear and pursue the children through a kitchen, but they escape and join the paleontologist and the paleobotanist.
The group reaches the control room, and one of the grandchildren restores the park's systems, allowing them to contact the industrialist, who radios for a helicopter to take them off the island.
The survivors are cornered by the two raptors in the visitor center, but the Tyrannosaurus appears and fights the raptors, allowing the group to flee.
The paleontologist and the industrialist agree not to endorse the park, and the group leaves the island in the helicopter.
In the lands of an eastern region, a pride of lions rules over the kingdom from a rock.
The king and queen's newborn son is presented to the gathered animals by a mandrill who is the kingdom's shaman and advisor.
The king's younger brother covets the throne and plots to eliminate the king and the prince so that he may become king.
When the prince grows into a young cub, the king shows him the kingdom and forbids him to explore beyond its borders.
The king explains to the prince the responsibilities of kingship and the "circle of life," which connects all living things.
The uncle manipulates the prince into exploring an elephants' graveyard beyond the kingdom.
There, the prince and his best friend are chased by three spotted hyenas.
The king is alerted by his majordomo, a hornbill, and rescues the cubs.
Though disappointed in the prince for disobeying him and endangering himself and his best friend, the king forgives him.
He explains that the great kings of the past watch over them from the night sky, from which he will one day watch over the prince.
The uncle visits the hyenas and convinces them to help him kill the king and the prince in exchange for hunting rights in the kingdom.
The uncle lures the prince into a gorge and signals the hyenas to drive a large herd of wildebeest into a stampede to trample him.
He then alerts the king, who saves the prince and tries to escape the gorge, but the uncle betrays him by throwing him into the stampede to his death.
As the prince mourns his father, the uncle deceives him into believing that the king's death was his fault and tells him to leave the kingdom and never return.
He orders the hyenas to kill the prince, but the prince escapes.
Unaware of the prince's survival, the uncle tells the pride that the stampede killed both the king and the prince, and steps forward as the new king, allowing the hyenas into the kingdom.
The prince collapses in a desert but is rescued by two outcasts, a meerkat and a warthog.
The prince grows up with his two new friends in their oasis, living a carefree life under their motto "hakuna matata" ("no worries" in Swahili).
Years later, an adult prince rescues the meerkat and the warthog from a hungry lioness, who is revealed to be his best friend.

The prince and his best friend fall in love with each other on their night out, and she urges him to return home, telling him that the kingdom has recently become stricken by a severe drought under the uncle's reign.
Still feeling guilty over the king's death, the prince refuses and leaves angrily.
He encounters the mandrill, who tells the prince that the king's spirit lives on in him.
The prince is visited by the spirit of the king in the night sky, who tells him that he must take his place as king.
After the mandrill advises him to learn from the past instead of running from it, the prince decides to return to the kingdom.
Aided by his friends, the prince sneaks past the hyenas at the rock and confronts the uncle, who shames the prince over his supposed role in the king's death.
Nearly backing the prince off a cliff, the uncle whispers that he killed the king.
Enraged, the prince retaliates and forces the uncle to confess the truth to the pride.
A battle ensues between the prince and his allies and the hyenas.
The uncle attempts to escape but is cornered by the prince at the top of the rock.
The uncle begs for mercy and falsely blames his actions on the hyenas.
The prince orders the uncle to leave the kingdom forever; the uncle seems to accept, but underhandedly attacks the prince.
Following a brief battle, the prince throws the uncle off the ledge.
The uncle survives the fall, but the hyenas, who overheard his betrayal, maul him to death.
With the uncle and the hyenas gone, the prince takes his place as king, and his best friend becomes his queen.
With the kingdom restored, the mandrill presents the new king and queen's newborn cub to the assembled animals, thus continuing the circle of life.
In 1985, a teenager lives in a town with his depressed alcoholic mother; his older siblings, who are professional and social failures; and his meek father, who is bullied by his supervisor.
After the teenager's band fails a music audition, he confides in his girlfriend that he fears becoming like his parents despite his ambitions.
That night, the teenager meets his eccentric scientist friend in a mall parking lot.
The scientist unveils a time machine built from a modified car, powered by plutonium he swindled from Libyan terrorists.
After the scientist inputs a destination time of November 5, 1955 (the day he conceived his time travel invention), the terrorists arrive unexpectedly and gun him down.
The teenager flees in the time machine, inadvertently activating time travel when reaching 88 miles per hour (142 kilometers per hour).
Arriving in 1955, the teenager discovers he has no plutonium, so he cannot return to 1985.
While exploring the burgeoning town, the teenager encounters his teenage father, discovering the bully was bullying the father even then.
The father falls into the path of an oncoming car while spying on the teenage mother changing clothes, and the teenager is knocked unconscious while saving him.
He wakes to find himself tended to by his mother, who becomes infatuated with him.
The teenager tracks down and convinces the younger scientist that he is from the future.
The scientist explains the only source available in 1955 capable of generating the 1.21 gigawatts of power required for time travel is a lightning bolt.
The teenager shows the scientist a flyer from the future that documents an upcoming lightning strike at the town's courthouse.

As the teenager's siblings begin to fade from a photo he carries with him, the scientist realizes the teenager's actions are altering the future and jeopardizing his existence: the mother was supposed to tend to the father instead of the teenager after the car accident.
Early attempts to get his parents acquainted fail, the teenager gains the animosity of the bully, and the mother's infatuation with the teenager deepens.

The mother asks the teenager to the school dance, and he plots to feign inappropriate advances on her, allowing the father to intervene and rescue her, but the plan goes awry when the bully's gang locks the teenager in the trunk of the performing band's car, while the bully forces himself onto the mother.
The father arrives expecting to find the teenager but is assaulted by the bully.
After the bully hurts the mother, an enraged father knocks him unconscious and escorts the grateful mother to the dance.
The band frees the teenager from their car, but the lead guitarist injures his hand in the process, so the teenager takes his place, performing while the father and the mother share their first kiss.
With his future no longer in jeopardy, the teenager hurries to the courthouse to meet the scientist.
The scientist discovers a letter from the teenager warning him about his future and rips it up, worried about the consequences.
To save the scientist, the teenager recalibrates the time machine to return ten minutes before he had left the future.
The lightning strikes, sending the teenager back to 1985, but the time machine breaks down, forcing the teenager to run back to the mall.
He arrives as the scientist is being shot.
While the teenager grieves at his side, the scientist sits up, revealing he had pieced the teenager's note back together and is wearing a bulletproof vest.
He takes the teenager home and departs to 2015 in the time machine.

The teenager wakes the next morning, discovering his father is now a confident and successful science fiction author, his mother is fit and happy, his siblings are successful, and the bully is a servile valet in his father's employ.
As the teenager reunites with his girlfriend, the scientist suddenly reappears in the time machine, insisting they return with him to the future to help their children.
A race of diminutive aliens visits the planet at night to gather plant specimens in a forest.
One of them separates from the group before government agents arrive.
The aliens depart before the agents can find them, leaving their lone member behind.
The creature takes shelter in a shed belonging to the family of a ten-year-old boy.
Initially scared by the creature, who runs away, the boy spends the following day leaving a trail of candy to lure the alien back to the family's home, where he hides it in his room.
The following morning, the boy feigns illness to stay home from school and play with the creature, whom he gives a name.
The boy introduces the alien to his older brother and five-year-old sister, who agree to keep the alien hidden from their single mother.

When the children ask about his origins, the alien displays telekinetic abilities by levitating several balls to represent his planetary system and later revives a dead chrysanthemum and instantly heals a cut on the boy's finger.
As the boy and the creature bond, they share thoughts and emotions.
At school, the boy becomes intoxicated because, at home, the alien is drinking beer.

Sensing the alien's desire to be rescued, the boy frees the frogs about to be vivisected in his biology class and kisses a girl he likes because the alien is watching an actor kiss an actress in a film.
Inspired by a comic strip depicting the character calling for help with a communication device, the alien builds a makeshift device to "phone home", using parts around the family home.
He also learns to speak English and requests the children's help to build the device.
On Halloween, the boy sneaks the alien into the forest, where they set up the device to call the alien's people.
The boy begs the alien to stay on the planet with him before falling asleep and waking alone in the forest the next day.
The boy returns home to his worried family while his brother searches for the alien, finding him pale and weakened in a culvert.
The brother takes the alien home, where the boy is also growing weaker, and reveals the creature to their mother just before government agents invade and quarantine the house.
The lead agent asks for the boy's help to save the alien.
However, the alien dies while the boy rapidly recovers.
Left alone to say goodbye, the boy tells the alien that he loves him.
The alien's heart begins to glow, and he is revived and restored to health.
The alien tells the boy that his people are returning for him.
The boy and his brother flee with the alien in a government vehicle.
They abandon the vehicle in a playground where they meet up with the brother’s friends who await on bikes with two extra bikes for the boy and his brother.
Together they all bike towards the forest, evading pursuing authorities who are rapidly closing in on them.
Heading towards a roadblock, the alien levitates the boys to safety and lands them in the forest.
The alien's ship arrives, and he says goodbye to the brother and the sister, who gifts him the chrysanthemum he previously revived.
The alien places his glowing finger on the boy's head and tells him that he will always be there.
The children, the mother, and the lead agent observe as the ship blasts off into space, leaving a rainbow in the sky.
In 1947, a banker arrives at a state prison to serve two consecutive life sentences for murdering his wife and her lover.
He is befriended by a contraband smuggler serving a life sentence, who procures for him a rock hammer and a large poster of an actress.
Assigned to work in the prison laundry, the banker is frequently raped by a gang, led by a ringleader.
In 1949, the banker overhears the captain of the guards complaining about being taxed on an inheritance and offers to help him shelter the money legally.
After the gang beat the banker to near-death, the captain cripples the ringleader, who is subsequently transferred to a minimum-security hospital; the banker is not attacked again.

The warden assigns the banker to the prison's decrepit library, ostensibly to assist an elderly inmate, but in reality, to use the banker's financial expertise in managing the warden's and other prison staff's finances.
The banker also starts writing weekly letters to the state legislature, requesting funding to improve the library.
The elderly inmate is paroled in 1954 after serving 50 years, but cannot adjust to the outside world and eventually hangs himself.

After years of the banker's ceaseless letters, the legislature sends a library donation that includes a recording of an opera; the banker plays an excerpt over the public address system, experiencing a moment of personal freedom before he is punished with solitary confinement.
After his release, the banker explains to a dismissive smuggler that hope is what gets him through his sentence.
In 1963, the warden begins exploiting prison labor for public works, profiting by undercutting skilled labor costs and receiving bribes.
The banker launders the money using an alias.
In 1965, the banker and the smuggler befriend a young inmate convicted of burglary.

The banker helps the young inmate pass his educational exam, and the young inmate later reveals that his cellmate at another prison confessed to committing the murders for which the banker was convicted.
When the banker informs the warden, the warden refuses to act.
Although the banker promises to keep the money laundering a secret, the warden sends the banker to solitary confinement and has the captain kill the young inmate under the guise of an escape attempt.
The warden then threatens to destroy the library, strip the banker of guard protection, and transfer him to harsher conditions if the banker refuses to continue with the money-laundering scheme.
A disheveled banker is released from solitary confinement after two months.
He tells a skeptical smuggler that he dreams of living in a town on the Mexican coast, where he can start anew.
He asks the smuggler to promise, once the smuggler is released, to travel to a specific hayfield near a town and recover a package that the banker buried there.
The smuggler worries that the banker is suicidal, especially after learning that he asked a fellow inmate for a rope.
At the next day's roll call, the guards find the banker's cell empty.
An irate warden throws a stone at a poster of an actress hanging on the cell wall, revealing a tunnel that the banker had dug with his rock hammer over 19 years.
The previous night, the banker escaped through the tunnel and prison sewage pipe, taking with him the warden's suit, shoes, and the ledger containing evidence of the corruption at the prison.
While guards search for him, the banker poses as his alias and withdraws over $370,000 of the laundered money from various banks, before mailing the ledger to a local newspaper.
State police arrive at the prison and take the captain into custody, while the warden kills himself to avoid arrest.
The following year, the smuggler is paroled after serving 40 years, but struggles to adapt to life outside prison and fears that he never will.
Remembering his promise to the banker, he visits the town and finds a cache containing money and a letter inviting him to come to the coastal town.
The smuggler violates his parole by traveling abroad, admitting that he finally feels hope.
He finds the banker on a beach, and the reunited friends happily embrace.
On February 1, a cynical television weatherman reassures his viewers that an approaching blizzard will miss the region.
Alongside his new producer and a cameraman, the weatherman travels to a town for his annual coverage of the groundhog festivities.
He makes no secret of his contempt for the assignment, the small town, and the "hicks" who live there, asserting that he will soon leave his station for a new job.
On February 2, the weatherman awakens in the inn to a song playing on the clock radio.
He gives a half-hearted report on the groundhog and the festivities.
Contrary to his prediction, the blizzard strikes the area, preventing all travel, and although he desperately searches for a way to leave, he is forced to spend the night in the town.
The next morning, the weatherman again awakens to the same song and the same DJ banter on the radio in his room at the inn.
He experiences the previous day's events repeating exactly and believes he is experiencing déjà vu.
He again unsuccessfully attempts to leave the town and retires to bed, only to awaken on February 2 once more.
The weatherman realizes that he is trapped in a time loop of which no one else is aware.
He confides his situation to the producer, who directs him to a neurologist, who in turn directs him to a psychologist; neither can explain his experiences.
He gets drunk with two locals and then leads police on a high-speed car chase before being arrested and imprisoned; the next morning, the weatherman awakens in the inn once again.

Realizing that there are no consequences for his actions, the weatherman begins to spend his loops indulging in binge eating, one-night stands, and robbery, using his growing knowledge of the day's events and the town's residents to manipulate circumstances to his advantage.
He eventually focuses on seducing the sweet-natured producer, using the loops to learn more about her and exploit that knowledge.
No matter what steps he takes, the producer rebuffs his advances, particularly when the weatherman tells her he loves her; she asserts that he does not even know her.
The weatherman gradually becomes depressed and desperate for a way to escape the loop.
He commits suicide in a variety of ways, including kidnapping the groundhog and driving them both off a cliff.
Each time, he reawakens on February 2.
He tries to explain his situation to the producer again, using his detailed knowledge of the day to predict events accurately.
Convinced, the producer spends the day with him and encourages him to view the loop as a blessing rather than a curse.
As they lie on the bed together at night, the weatherman realizes that his feelings for the producer have become sincere.
He wakes alone on February 2.
He decides to use the loop to change himself and help others: he saves people from deadly accidents and misfortunes and learns to play the piano, sculpt ice, and speak French.
Despite his efforts, however, he is haunted by his inability to prevent a homeless old man from dying of natural causes.
During one iteration of the loop, the weatherman reports on the groundhog festivities with such eloquence that other news crews stop working to listen, amazing the producer.
The weatherman continues his day helping the people of the town.
That night, the producer witnesses the weatherman's expert piano-playing as the adoring townsfolk regale her with stories of his good deeds.
Impressed by his apparent overnight transformation, the producer successfully bids for him at a charity bachelor auction.
The weatherman carves an ice sculpture in the producer's image and tells her that no matter what happens, even if he is trapped in the loop forever, he is finally happy because he loves her.
They share a kiss and retire to his room.
The weatherman wakes the next morning to find the producer still in bed with him; it is now February 3.
He tells the producer he wants to live in the town with her.
After being homeschooled her entire life and having spent the last twelve years abroad, a 16-year-old girl begins her first day at a high school.

She struggles to make friends and is patronized by the teachers, but befriends an outcast and her friend, who explain the school's various cliques to her and warn her about one clique, a trio of wealthy mean girls consisting of a ruthless queen bee, an insecure gossiper, and a bubbly airhead.
The queen bee, the gossiper, and the airhead take a shine to the new girl and unexpectedly invite her to join the clique.
Upon realizing this, the outcast hatches a plan to infiltrate the group and destroy the queen bee's reputation.
The new girl becomes infatuated with a classmate.
The airhead and the gossiper reveal that the classmate is the queen bee's ex-boyfriend and thus is off-limits, though the queen bee claims not to care if the new girl and the classmate date.
Despite the outcast's warnings, the new girl comes to enjoy hanging out with the group, including writing insulting remarks about their classmates and teachers in a scrapbook.
At a Halloween house party, the queen bee promises to talk to the classmate on the new girl's behalf, but instead kisses him in front of her and resumes their relationship.
Enraged, the new girl fully commits to the outcast's plan.

Over the following months, the new girl, with the outcast and her friend's help, manages to trick the gossiper into divulging secrets, sabotage the queen bee's relationship with the classmate (and spend time with him by pretending to need math tutoring, despite being mathematically gifted), and cause the queen bee to gain weight by giving her high-calorie snack bars under the pretense that they are diet food.
After violating the clique's dress code rules by wearing sweatpants on Monday due to her weight gain, the queen bee is ousted from the group, as the new girl replaces her as "queen bee".
While the new girl's parents are out of town, she throws a house party, during which she drunkenly admits to the classmate that she does not actually need math tutoring.
He derides her for being as manipulative as the queen bee.
The outcast and her friend angrily confront the new girl for throwing a party instead of attending the former's art show and declare that she has become as fake as she pretended to be.
Meanwhile, the queen bee discovers the truth about the snack bars and inserts slander of herself into the scrapbook, hoping to frame the new girl and the other clique members.
The queen bee spreads the book's pages throughout the hallways, inciting chaos.
The principal and the math teacher gather the female junior students in the gym to talk through their social issues.
During this, the outcast publicly admits her plan to destroy the queen bee and openly mocks her, much to the other students' excitement.
The queen bee furiously storms out, pursued by an apologetic new girl.
While ranting at the new girl, the queen bee is hit by a school bus, fracturing her spine.
Rumors circulate that the new girl intentionally pushed the queen bee in front of the bus, resulting her in becoming a social pariah and grounded by her parents.

After realizing a comment she wrote in the scrapbook has framed the math teacher as a drug dealer, causing police to visit the school and interrogate her math class, the new girl decides to take full responsibility for the book.
The queen bee, the gossiper, and the airhead are spared punishment.
To earn extra credit, the new girl joins the math team, moderated by the math teacher and led by a fellow student.
At the state finals, she correctly answers the tiebreaker question, winning the championship.
The team arrives at the spring dance, where the new girl is elected queen, to her surprise.
She breaks her tiara and distributes the pieces to others in the crowd, making peace with the outcast, her friend, and the clique.
She later shares a slow dance and kiss with the classmate.
The clique disbands by the time senior year begins.
A fully recovered queen bee joins the school's lacrosse team to channel her anger positively, the gossiper joins another clique, and the airhead becomes the school's weather girl.
The new girl begins dating the classmate and continues to hang out with the outcast and her friend, the former of whom starts dating the team leader.

While reflecting on the relative social peace that has taken over the school, the new girl notices a new popular clique in the freshman class and wonders how long the junior clique will last, imagining them being hit by a school bus.
